_note: Entries that also exist in The Law Tome. Generated by `npm run crosswalk` from both corpora; committed because CI checks out this repository alone. A name match is taken as-is. An alias match counts only when an alias HERE equals the canonical name THERE: alias-to-alias paired escalation of commitment with the sunk cost fallacy, which this corpus says are different things, and their-alias-to-our-name paired authority bias with the Milgram experiment.

tome.name: The Sunk Cost Fallacy
tome.statement: We keep going because of what we've already spent, which we can never get back.

tome.name: The Dunning–Kruger Effect
tome.statement: The skills you need to do a task well are the same skills you need to know you are doing it badly.

tome.name: Confirmation Bias
tome.statement: We seek, read, and remember evidence that confirms what we already believe.

tome.name: The Anchoring Effect
tome.statement: The first number you hear drags your estimate toward it, even when it's irrelevant.

tome.name: The Framing Effect
tome.statement: The same choice, described as a gain or a loss, draws opposite decisions.

tome.name: Survivorship Bias
tome.statement: Studying only the winners misleads you, because the losers vanished from view.

tome.name: The Pygmalion Effect
tome.statement: Higher expectations of a person tend to raise their performance.

tome.name: The False-Consensus Effect
tome.statement: People assume their own views and habits are far more common than they really are.

tome.name: The Fundamental Attribution Error
tome.statement: We blame others' behaviour on their character and our own on the circumstances.

tome.name: The Affect Heuristic
tome.statement: People judge risks and benefits by consulting their immediate gut feeling toward something rather than analyzing it.

tome.name: The Forer Effect
tome.statement: Vague descriptions that fit almost anyone feel uncannily personal.

tome.name: The Mere-Exposure Effect
tome.statement: The more often we encounter something, the more we tend to like it.

tome.name: The Spotlight Effect
tome.statement: We think everyone noticed our stumble or stain, but far fewer did than we imagine.

tome.name: The Halo Effect
tome.statement: One good impression bleeds into judgements of unrelated qualities.

tome.name: Cognitive Dissonance
tome.statement: Holding clashing beliefs feels uncomfortable, so we change one to ease the tension.

tome.name: The Gambler's Fallacy
tome.statement: Believing a run of one outcome makes the opposite 'due' in independent trials.

tome.name: The Hawthorne Effect
tome.statement: People change their behaviour when they know they are being watched.

tome.name: The Illusory Truth Effect
tome.statement: Repeat a claim often enough and it starts to feel true, whether or not it is.

tome.name: The Curse of Knowledge
tome.statement: Once you know something, you cannot imagine what it is like not to know it.

tome.name: The Just-World Hypothesis
tome.statement: People need to believe the world is fair, so they decide victims must deserve their fate.

tome.name: The Zeigarnik Effect
tome.statement: People remember unfinished tasks better than completed ones.

tome.name: Loss Aversion
tome.statement: Losses hurt more than equivalent gains please.

tome.name: The Impostor Phenomenon
tome.statement: People who are demonstrably competent can persistently believe their success is a fraud they have not yet been found out for.

tome.name: The Baader–Meinhof Phenomenon
tome.statement: Once you notice something, you start seeing it everywhere.

tome.name: Groupthink
tome.statement: When a group prizes harmony over honest appraisal, it talks itself into bad decisions.

tome.name: The Base Rate Fallacy
tome.statement: Judging a case on its specifics while ignoring how common it is to begin with.

tome.name: The Availability Heuristic
tome.statement: We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

tome.name: The Negativity Bias
tome.statement: Bad events, emotions, and news hit us harder than equally strong good ones.

tome.name: The Planning Fallacy
tome.statement: We underestimate how long things will take, even knowing how long they took last time.

tome.name: The Endowment Effect
tome.statement: We value a thing more once we own it.

tome.name: The Hindsight Bias
tome.statement: Once you know how it turned out, it feels as if you knew it all along.

tome.name: The IKEA Effect
tome.statement: We value the things we build ourselves more than they are objectively worth.

tome.name: The Optimism Bias
tome.statement: We expect good things to happen to us and bad things to happen to other people.

tome.name: Status Quo Bias
tome.statement: People disproportionately prefer keeping their current state of affairs over switching to an alternative, even a better one.

tome.name: The Texas Sharpshooter Fallacy
tome.statement: Fire wildly, then draw the bullseye around the tightest cluster and call yourself a marksman.

tome.name: Berkson's Paradox
tome.statement: Two unrelated traits can look negatively correlated within a group selected on having at least one of them.

tome.name: The Stroop Effect
tome.statement: Naming the ink colour of a word is slow and error-prone when the word spells a different colour.

tome.name: The Bandwagon Effect
tome.statement: The more people adopt something, the more others adopt it, just because others have.

tome.name: The Peak-End Rule
tome.statement: We judge an experience by its most intense moment and its ending, not its whole.

tome.name: The Overconfidence Effect
tome.statement: People's confidence in their own judgements is reliably greater than the accuracy of those judgements.

tome.name: Hyperbolic Discounting
tome.statement: The future's pull weakens sharply up close and gently far off, so plans flip.

tome.name: The Spiral of Silence
tome.statement: Fearing isolation, people who sense they hold the minority view fall silent, making the majority seem even larger.

tome.name: Mean World Syndrome
tome.statement: Heavy exposure to violent media content cultivates an exaggerated belief that the world is more dangerous than it actually is.

tome.name: The Law of the Instrument
tome.statement: If the only tool you have is a hammer, everything starts to look like a nail.

tome.name: The Testing Effect
tome.statement: Retrieving a fact from memory fixes it better than reading it again.

tome.name: The Spacing Effect
tome.statement: Study spread over time sticks; study crammed into one session fades.

tome.name: The Illusion of Control
tome.statement: People systematically overestimate their ability to control events that are actually determined by chance.

tome.name: The Decoy Effect
tome.statement: Add a third option no one picks, and it pushes the choice toward its neighbour.

tome.name: The Self-Serving Bias
tome.statement: We take credit for our successes and blame our failures on everything else.

tome.name: The Von Restorff Effect
tome.statement: The one thing that stands out from the rest is the one you remember.

tome.name: The Google Effect
tome.statement: We forget facts we believe we can look up, remembering instead where to find them.

tome.name: The Pratfall Effect
tome.statement: A small blunder makes a highly competent person more likable, but makes an average one less so.

tome.name: The Peltzman Effect
tome.statement: Making something safer leads people to behave more riskily, offsetting part of the gain.

tome.name: The Semmelweis Reflex
tome.statement: New evidence is reflexively rejected when it contradicts established beliefs, norms, or paradigms.

tome.name: Moral Luck
tome.statement: We praise and blame people for things partly beyond their control, which seems to violate a basic principle.

tome.name: The Reciprocity Norm
tome.statement: Give someone a favour, even an unasked one, and they feel an obligation to give one back.

tome.name: The Milgram Experiment
tome.statement: Ordinary people, ordered by an authority, kept delivering shocks they thought were harming a stranger.

tome.name: The Picture Superiority Effect
tome.statement: We remember pictures far better than the same ideas presented as words.

tome.name: The Weber–Fechner Law
tome.statement: Perceived intensity grows with the logarithm of the stimulus, so we sense proportion, not amount.

tome.name: The Overjustification Effect
tome.statement: Pay people for something they already loved doing, and their inner motivation for it can wither.

tome.name: The Clever Hans Effect
tome.statement: An observer's own unconscious cues can lead a subject (human or animal) to produce responses the observer subtly expects.

tome.name: The Representativeness Heuristic
tome.statement: People judge the probability of something by how closely it resembles a typical example, ignoring actual base rates.

tome.name: The Bystander Effect
tome.statement: The more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them helps.

tome.name: The Cocktail Party Effect
tome.statement: In a noisy room you can lock onto one conversation, yet your own name in another still snaps your attention.

tome.name: The Actor-Observer Bias
tome.statement: People tend to attribute their own actions to the situation but others' identical actions to enduring disposition.

tome.name: The Paradox of Choice
tome.statement: Some choice is good, but too many options can paralyze and dissatisfy rather than liberate.

tome.name: The Marshmallow Test
tome.statement: A child offered one treat now or two if they wait reveals a capacity for delayed gratification, once thought to predict success.

tome.name: The Backfire Effect
tome.statement: The claim that correcting a falsehood makes people believe it more, which mostly does not hold.

tome.name: The Third-Person Effect
tome.statement: People think persuasive media sway everyone else far more than they sway themselves.

tome.name: Illusory Correlation
tome.statement: People perceive a relationship between two variables or events even when no real relationship exists in the data they observed.

tome.name: Social Facilitation
tome.statement: People often perform simple or well-learned tasks better, but complex tasks worse, in the presence of others.

tome.name: Functional Fixedness
tome.statement: People fixate on an object's conventional use, which blocks them from seeing how it could solve a problem in an unconventional way.

tome.name: Naïve Realism
tome.statement: People assume they see reality objectively and conclude that those who disagree must be uninformed, irrational, or biased.

tome.name: The Horn Effect
tome.statement: One bad trait colours the whole judgement: a person seen as failing in one respect is assumed to be failing in others.

tome.name: The Money Illusion
tome.statement: People judge money by its face value and forget that inflation quietly shrinks what it buys.

tome.name: The Ellsberg Paradox
tome.statement: People will pay to avoid unknown odds, preferring a known gamble even when it cannot be squared with any consistent belief.

tome.name: The Allais Paradox
tome.statement: People who take a sure million over a gamble will still gamble when both options become uncertain, defying expected utility.

tome.name: Belief Perseverance
tome.statement: People tend to keep holding a belief even after the evidence that originally supported it has been thoroughly discredited.

tome.name: The Illusion of Transparency
tome.statement: People believe their inner nerves, feelings, and lies show on the outside far more than they really do.

tome.name: The Hostile Media Effect
tome.statement: Opposing partisans watch the same neutral news report and each side is sure it is biased against them.

tome.name: The Aesthetic-Usability Effect
tome.statement: People perceive more beautiful designs as easier to use, and forgive their flaws.

tome.name: The Scarcity Principle
tome.statement: People want a thing more when it is rare or slipping out of reach.

tome.name: The Ben Franklin Effect
tome.statement: Doing someone a favour makes you like them more, not the other way round.

tome.name: The Matthew Effect
tome.statement: To those who have, more is given: advantage accumulates and the eminent gain more than their share.

tome.name: Parkinson's Law of Triviality
tome.statement: The time a committee spends on an item is inversely proportional to the money involved.

tome.name: The Stanford Prison Experiment
tome.statement: Students playing guards turned cruel in a mock prison, in a study now largely discredited.

tome.name: Learned Helplessness
tome.statement: An animal or person repeatedly subjected to unavoidable harm stops trying to escape, even when escape becomes possible.

tome.name: Deindividuation
tome.statement: Submerged in a crowd and stripped of identity, people do things they never would alone.

tome.name: The Ringelmann Effect
tome.statement: As a group grows, each member pulls less of their own weight.

tome.name: Inattentional Blindness
tome.statement: Absorbed in one task, people can miss something as obvious as a gorilla in plain sight.

tome.name: The Rosenhan Experiment
tome.statement: Healthy people who faked a single symptom were admitted to psychiatric hospitals and diagnosed as mentally ill.

tome.name: Change Blindness
tome.statement: A large change to a scene can go unnoticed if it happens during a blink, cut, or flicker.

tome.name: The Uncanny Valley
tome.statement: A figure that looks almost but not quite human tips from endearing into deeply unsettling.

tome.name: The Straw Man
tome.statement: Beat a distorted, feeble version of your opponent's argument and pretend you've defeated the real one.

tome.name: The Ad Hominem
tome.statement: Attack the person making an argument instead of answering the argument itself.

tome.name: The Red Herring
tome.statement: Throw in something irrelevant to distract from the real question rather than answer it.

tome.name: The No True Scotsman
tome.statement: When a counterexample refutes your generalization, redefine the category so it no longer counts.

tome.name: Begging the Question
tome.statement: Assume the very thing you are trying to prove, so the argument proves nothing.

tome.name: The False Dilemma
tome.statement: Present only two options as if they were the only ones, when in fact more exist.

tome.name: The Slippery Slope
tome.statement: Claim one small step must lead, unstoppably, to some disastrous end, without showing why.

tome.name: Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc
tome.statement: Assuming that because event Y followed event X, X must have caused Y.

tome.name: The Appeal to Authority
tome.statement: Cite an authority's say-so as proof, even when they are no expert or the point is theirs to assert.

tome.name: The Loaded Question
tome.statement: A question is phrased so that any direct answer concedes a controversial, unproven assumption.

tome.name: The Trolley Problem
tome.statement: Most would divert a runaway trolley to kill one instead of five, but few would push a man to do the same.

tome.name: The Sorites Paradox
tome.statement: One grain isn't a heap, and adding one never makes a heap, yet heaps exist.

tome.name: The Naturalistic Fallacy
tome.statement: You cannot define good as any natural property; that goodness just is pleasure or the like is a fallacy.

tome.name: The Appeal to Nature
tome.statement: Assume something is good because it is natural, or bad because it is unnatural.

tome.name: The Is-Ought Problem
tome.statement: You cannot logically derive what ought to be from what merely is; facts alone do not entail values.

tome.name: Poisoning the Well
tome.statement: Poisoning the well discredits a speaker in advance by presenting negative information about them before they can speak.

tome.name: Moving the Goalposts
tome.statement: Moving the goalposts means changing the criteria for success partway through, after the original criteria have already been met.

tome.name: The Genetic Fallacy
tome.statement: Judge a claim by where it came from rather than by whether it is actually true.

tome.name: Equivocation
tome.statement: An argument secretly shifts the meaning of an ambiguous word between its premises and conclusion.

tome.name: The Nirvana Fallacy
tome.statement: The nirvana fallacy rejects a workable solution by comparing it only to an idealized, unrealistic alternative rather than the real options.

tome.name: The Lump of Labour Fallacy
tome.statement: There is no fixed amount of work to share out, so one group working more need not leave less for others.

tome.name: The Elaboration Likelihood Model
tome.statement: Persuasion travels one of two roads: careful thought about the argument, or a quick reaction to surface cues.

tome.name: Flashbulb Memory
tome.statement: A shocking, consequential event can imprint a vivid, confidently held memory of the moment one learned of it, though not necessarily an accurate one.

tome.name: The McGurk Effect
tome.statement: What you see a mouth doing changes what you hear it say.

tome.name: The Yerkes–Dodson Law
tome.statement: Performance rises with arousal up to a point, then falls, and the peak comes sooner for harder tasks.

tome.name: The Foot-in-the-Door Technique
tome.statement: Agree to a small request first, and you become far more likely to grant a big one later.

tome.name: The Rubber Hand Illusion
tome.statement: Watch a fake hand stroked in time with your hidden one, and your brain starts to feel the rubber hand is yours.

tome.name: The Broken Windows Theory
tome.statement: Visible disorder invites more disorder, and eventually serious crime.

tome.name: The Small-World Phenomenon
tome.statement: In a vast, mostly clustered social network, any two people are linked by a surprisingly short chain of acquaintances.

tome.name: The Strange Situation
tome.statement: By watching how an infant reacts to leaving and reunion, the procedure reveals the quality of its attachment.

tome.name: The Little Albert Experiment
tome.statement: By pairing a white rat with a frightening noise, researchers taught an infant to fear the rat and other furry things.

tome.name: The Bobo Doll Experiment
tome.statement: Children who watched an adult attack an inflatable doll went on to attack it the same way themselves.

tome.name: Special Pleading
tome.statement: Special pleading is applying a rule to everyone except oneself or one's group, without a logically relevant reason for the exemption.

tome.name: The Misinformation Effect
tome.statement: Misleading information encountered after an event can distort a person's memory of what they originally witnessed.

tome.name: The Fallacy Fallacy
tome.statement: A bad argument for a claim does not prove the claim false; the conclusion may still be true.

tome.name: The Courtier's Reply
tome.statement: The courtier's reply dismisses a critic by claiming they lack the credentials or expertise to criticize, without addressing the substance.

tome.name: The Serial Position Effect
tome.statement: We remember the first and last items on a list best, the middle worst.

tome.name: The Intentional Fallacy
tome.statement: Judging a work by what the author intended is a mistake: the meaning is in the text, not the mind.
